messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kaito is a 56-year-old detective who has built a four-decade career on a foundation of controlled, quiet observation. Now, that foundation is crumbling. He came to therapy after an incident at work where he froze during an interview with an assault victim, an experience that has left him suspended between intense rage and a profound sense of personal failure. For most of his life, Kaito believed he had successfully buried his childhood. He recalls his stepfather not as a person but as a series of sensory fragments: the acrid smell of a cigarette burning down to the filter, the rough texture of a flannel shirt, and the sharp, searing pain of being burned for minor infractions. These were not memories he revisited, but a sealed part of his history that he had learned never to touch.

The seal broke six months ago during a fire investigation. The smell of burnt upholstery hung in the air, and without warning, Kaito was no longer a detective at a crime scene but a small boy, cornered and terrified. The memory was not a narrative but a physical assault of rage and helplessness that left him dizzy and short of breath. Since then, these intrusions have become relentless, triggered by seemingly innocuous cues. Because the memory now returns with such visceral, unpredictable force, he finds himself constantly scanning his environment for anything that might set it off again, making previously neutral sights and smells feel laden with threat. Something in his surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning. This constant state of alert has destroyed his sleep; he lies awake for hours, convinced he needs to stay vigilant, his body coiled with a tension that never fully dissipates. This hypervigilance makes him exquisitely sensitive to new threats, and the more watchful he is, the more his environment seems to be seeded with reminders of the past.

These unpredictable memory intrusions generate a powerful sense of physical threat. When an image or sensation breaks through, Kaito’s heart hammers in his chest, and a cold sweat breaks out on his skin. This overwhelming physical reaction is terrifying to him; he has come to believe it is proof that he is mentally unraveling. His reactions since the event, he states, show that he is a "lousy coper." The intensity of the threat he feels in those moments reinforces his deepest-held negative beliefs about himself—that the abuse happened because of some intrinsic flaw in his character, and that his inability to control these reactions now is just further evidence of that flaw. This conviction that he is fundamentally broken means the memories are not just history, but an ongoing indictment of his worth.

The world has become a minefield. The sight of a victim who looks vulnerable, particularly a young person, can trigger a cascade of memories and an immediate, protective urge to withdraw. In response to these triggers, Kaito has developed a rigid set of rules to keep himself safe. He avoids people whenever possible, taking his lunch alone in his car and turning down the rare social invitation from colleagues. This isolation has become a habit, one that cost him his marriage years ago and is now alienating his current partner at the precinct. He finds himself detaching from his own mind when a memory starts to surface, a mental retreat that leaves him feeling numb and disconnected from his own life. These strategies, meant to control the distress, only deepen his conviction that he is weak and incapable. The more he avoids, the more proof he has that he cannot handle the world, and the more potent the memories become when they inevitably break through his defenses.

Even a moment of levity feels dangerous. A shared joke at the station or a rare feeling of peace on a quiet evening is immediately followed by a wave of anxiety, as if positive emotions are a foreign language his body can no longer understand. This confusion makes him retreat further, reinforcing the cycle of isolation. The strategies he uses to survive day-to-day—avoiding people, avoiding certain clothes, detaching from his feelings—have paradoxically made him more sensitive to triggers, not less. His world has shrunk to his job and his empty apartment. He sought help because his professional identity, the last bastion of his self-worth, is now threatened. He is terrified that the past he spent a lifetime outrunning has finally caught him, and that there is nothing left of the man he tried so hard to become.
